lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Welcome to a brand-new world. Last time, we found a map with a green leaf in the Amber Library. We opened the back door of the library, and look! We are in a big glass house full of plants. This is the Green Laboratory. A laboratory is a place for experiments. Many people say lab for short. Scientists study plants here. Say it with me. Scientists study plants here. Great job! Here comes the head scientist. He's a very old tortoise, and his name is Dr. Moss. He moves slowly, but he thinks fast. There's a sign on the wall. Let's read it. "Welcome to the Green Laboratory. Here, we ask questions about nature. We look closely, we measure carefully, and we write down everything. Please do not touch the Sleeping Seed." Hmm, the Sleeping Seed? What's that? Dr. Moss says, It's a very old seed. It never opened. Maybe you can help me someday. Now, phonics. Microscope. Microphone. Microwave. Microchip. Micro means small. A microscope helps us see small things. Let's start our science adventure!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Before we do any experiments, we need to learn the lab rules. Safety first! Dr. Moss is holding a pair of goggles. Goggles protect your eyes. Wear your goggles. Don't touch the hot plate. Say it with me. Wear your goggles. Don't touch the hot plate. Very good! When we tell someone a safety rule, we start with a verb. Wear. Don't touch. Wash. And we can say need to. We need to wash our hands after the experiment. Let's read the safety poster together. "Lab Safety Rules. One: Always ask an adult first. Two: Wear your goggles. Three: Don't touch the hot plate. Four: Never taste anything in the lab. Five: Wash your hands after the experiment. Six: If something spills, tell an adult right away." Great reading! Rule number four is very important. Some things look like juice, but they are not juice! Now, phonics. Telescope. Periscope. Kaleidoscope. Stethoscope. Scope means a tool for looking. A telescope helps us look at faraway stars. Let's be safe scientists!

phonics.tipJa: meter は「はかる どうぐ」の いみの パーツ。thermometer（おんどけい＝ねつを はかる）、speedometer（スピードメーター＝はやさを はかる）、pedometer（まんぽけい＝あるいた あしの かずを はかる）、barometer（きあつけい）。まんなかの o は つなぎの もじ。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will use a real microscope. Dr. Moss puts a tiny piece of a leaf on a glass slide. Now, look through the microscope. Turn the knob slowly. What can you see? I can see tiny circles! Say it with me. I can see tiny circles! Wonderful! To say more, use looks like. It looks like a green honeycomb. These tiny circles are the parts of the leaf. We call them cells. Every plant has many, many cells. Let's read Dr. Moss's note about the microscope. "This microscope makes things look one hundred times bigger. A leaf looks flat and smooth to your eyes. But under the microscope, you can see many small green boxes and circles. Plants are full of tiny surprises!" Isn't that amazing? Remember, use short sentences. I can see. It looks like. It's green. Now, phonics. Thermometer. Speedometer. Pedometer. Barometer. Meter means a tool for measuring. A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is. Next time, we will use one! Let's look closely like real scientists!

phonics.tipJa: thermo は「ねつ・あたたかさ」。thermometer は thermo（ねつ）＋ meter（はかる どうぐ）＝おんどけい。thermostat は おんどを たもつ スイッチ。microscope は micro（ちいさい）＋ scope（みる どうぐ）、telescope は tele（とおく）＋ scope。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Scientists measure things carefully. Today, we will use a thermometer and a ruler. First, put the thermometer in the cup of water. Wait for ten seconds. Now, read the number. The water is 20 degrees. Say it with me. The water is 20 degrees. Good! Next, the ruler. How long is this leaf? It's 15 centimeters long. When you measure, start at zero, and hold the ruler straight. Scientists always check. Let's measure it again to check. Here is a page from Dr. Moss's measuring notebook. Let's read it. "Monday morning. The water in the fish tank was 20 degrees. The big leaf was 15 centimeters long. The small leaf was 6 centimeters long. Monday afternoon. The water was 23 degrees. The sun made it warmer." So, the morning and the afternoon were different. Numbers help us see changes. Now, phonics. Microscope. Telescope. Thermometer. Thermostat. Thermo means heat. Meter means a tool for measuring. Put them together, and you get thermometer! Let's measure everything!

phonics.tipJa: パーツの まとめ: micro（ちいさい）・scope（みる どうぐ）・meter（はかる どうぐ）・thermo（ねつ）。microphone・periscope・pedometer・thermometer。パーツが わかると、はじめての どうぐの なまえも よそうできる！

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Every scientist has a lab notebook. Today, we will learn how to write one. Dr. Moss writes in his notebook every day. A good page has four parts. The date. What I did. What I saw. And a picture. Here's a new word. Observe. Observe means to look very carefully. Today, I observed a leaf. Say it with me. Today, I observed a leaf. Excellent! Let's read Haru's notebook page. "Date: May 12. Today, I observed a leaf. I used a microscope and a ruler. The leaf was 15 centimeters long. Under the microscope, I saw tiny green circles. They looked like a honeycomb. Question: Why are leaves green?" Wow, Haru even wrote a question. Scientists always have new questions. Use the past tense in your notebook, because you write after the experiment. I used. I saw. It was. Now, phonics review. Microphone. Periscope. Pedometer. Thermometer. Small, look, measure, heat. Now, write your first notebook page. Write four or five sentences, and draw a picture. Let's be careful observers!

phonics.tipJa: experiment（じっけん）・instrument（どうぐ・がっき）・document（しょるい）・ornament（かざり）。おわりの「メント」は よわく よむので「マント」「ミント」に きこえる ことも ある。でも つづりは いつも m・e・n・t。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will do our first experiment. Before an experiment, a scientist makes a guess. That's called a prediction. Predict means to say what will happen. Here's a big tank of water. Here's an apple. Will it float or sink? I predict the apple will float. Say it with me. I predict the apple will float. Wonderful! Now, ask your friend. What do you predict? You can also say I think. I think the stone will sink. Let's read the experiment card from Dr. Moss. "Float or Sink? You need: a tank of water, an apple, a stone, a coin, a leaf, a carrot and a plastic spoon. Step one: Hold each thing over the water. Step two: Write your prediction. Step three: Put it in the water gently. Step four: Write the result." Remember, a prediction is not right or wrong. It's just a smart guess. Scientists are happy when they are surprised! Now, phonics. Experiment. Instrument. Document. Ornament. The end is weak, so it sounds like ment, mant or mint. But the spelling is always m, e, n, t. Let's make predictions!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we made predictions. Today, we will observe. Dr. Moss gives us a glass of soda water and some raisins. Drop in three raisins and watch closely. What did you observe? I observed small bubbles. Say it with me. I observed small bubbles. Great! When you report, use the past tense, because the experiment is finished. I observed. I saw. They went up. The raisins went up and down. Let's read Kiko's observation notes. "First, the raisins sank to the bottom. After a minute, I observed small bubbles on the raisins. The bubbles carried the raisins up to the top. At the top, the bubbles popped, and the raisins went down again. They went up and down for ten minutes. They looked like little dancers!" Kiko's notes are very clear. She wrote what happened first, next and last. Now, phonics. Measurement. Arrangement. Amazement. Basement. Measure ends with e. Do we drop the e? No! Keep the e and add ment. Now, let's watch the dancing raisins and talk about what you observed!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today's experiment is about an egg. Here's a glass of water. Put the egg in the water gently. What happened? It sank to the bottom. Now, let's add salt. One spoon. Stir. Two spoons. Stir. Three, four, five, six... Nothing yet. More salt! Look! The egg is going up! The result was surprising. The egg floated! Say it with me. The result was surprising. The egg floated! Fantastic! The result is what happened in the end. Let's read the result part of Riko's report. "At first, the egg sank to the bottom of the glass. We added salt, one spoon at a time. After six spoons, nothing happened. After we added salt again and again, the egg slowly floated up to the top. Our prediction was wrong, and that was the best part!" I love that last sentence. When the result is different from the prediction, we learn something new. Now, phonics. Equipment. Development. Environment. Experiment. Equip and develop. Don't double the last letter. And don't forget the n in environment. Let's report our surprising results!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, the egg floated in salt water. But why did it happen? Scientists always ask why. Dr. Moss has two cups of water, the same size. One is fresh water. One is salt water. Let's put them on the scale. Look! The salt water is heavier. It happened because salt water is heavier. Say it with me. It happened because salt water is heavier. Good job! The heavy water pushes the egg up. Let's read about a real place. "The Dead Sea is a big lake in West Asia. Its water is very, very salty. It's much saltier than the ocean. When people go into the water, they float easily. Some people float on their backs and read a newspaper! The salty water pushes them up." Isn't that amazing? Now you know why. To give a reason, use because. The egg floated because the water was salty. Now, phonics review. Measurement. Equipment. Environment. Amazement. Keep the e in measurement and amazement. Don't double the p in equipment. Now, let's explain the reasons for our results!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today is report day. Each team will present one experiment. A good science report has four parts. The question. The prediction. The result. And the reason. When we talk about our prediction, we say predicted. We predicted the egg would sink. The result was different. Say it with me. We predicted the egg would sink. The result was different. Excellent! Remember, after predicted, will becomes would. Let's read Haru and Riko's poster. "Our question: Can an egg float? Our prediction: We predicted the egg would sink. What we did: We put an egg in water. Then we added salt, one spoon at a time. The result: The egg floated after many spoons of salt. The reason: It happened because salt water is heavier than fresh water." That's a perfect report. Speak slowly, look at the audience and point to your poster. At the end, ask, Do you have any questions? Now, phonics review. Experiment. Measurement. Equipment. Environment. Write them correctly on your poster. Let's give great reports!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will learn a new pattern for science. If you do something, something happens. Dr. Moss puts an ice cube in a pan. An adult turns on the hot plate. Look! The ice is getting smaller. If you heat ice, it melts. Say it with me. If you heat ice, it melts. Great job! Keep heating. The water is bubbling. If you heat water, it turns into steam. And here's a cold lid. If you cool steam, it turns back into water. Look at the drops on the lid! Let's read Dr. Moss's water poster. "Water can change its form. Ice is solid. You can hold it. Water is liquid. It flows. Steam is gas. It floats into the air. If you heat ice, it melts into water. If you heat water to 100 degrees Celsius, it boils and turns into steam. If you cool steam, it turns back into water." Water can change a lot! Remember, if plus the present, then the present. If you heat ice, it melts. Now, phonics. Photograph. Photography. Photographer. Photographic. Listen to the strong part move! Let's do the ice dance!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Here's a question. Does water get bigger or smaller when it freezes? Yesterday, Dr. Moss filled a plastic bottle with water and put it in the freezer. Let's open the freezer. Look at the bottle! The ice is coming out of the top! When water freezes, it gets bigger. Say it with me. When water freezes, it gets bigger. Excellent! When is like if. It shows something that always happens. When ice melts, it turns into water. Now, a safety rule. Don't put a glass bottle in the freezer. It can break! Let's read a winter story from Dr. Moss. "One cold night, the water in a pipe outside my lab froze. When water freezes, it gets bigger. The ice pushed and pushed, and the pipe cracked. In the morning, the sun came out. When the ice melted, water sprayed everywhere! Now, I always wrap my pipes in warm blankets in winter." Poor Dr. Moss! Now, phonics. Scientist. Scientific. Energy. Energetic. Listen. SCI-en-tist. sci-en-TIF-ic. The strong part moves! Let's be energetic scientists!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, our lab is full of colors. Dr. Moss gives us three cups of colored water. Red, blue and yellow. Scientists ask questions before they try something. What happens if we mix blue and yellow? Say it with me. What happens if we mix blue and yellow? Good! Now, let's try it and see. One drop of blue. One drop of yellow. Swirl the cup. It turns green! If you mix red and yellow, you get orange. Here's Dr. Moss's color chart. Let's read it. "Three colors can make many new colors. If you mix blue and yellow, you get green. If you mix red and yellow, you get orange. If you mix red and blue, you get purple. What happens if you mix all three? Try it and see! Write your answer in your lab notebook." Hmm, what do you think? Make a prediction first. Then try it. Remember, What happens if is a great question for every scientist. Now, phonics. Electric. Electricity. Biology. Biological. Listen. e-LEC-tric, e-lec-TRIC-i-ty. The strong part moves to the right. Let's mix some colors!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will test magnets. Dr. Moss has a box of things. A paper clip, a paper cup, an iron nail, a coin, a pencil, a steel can and an aluminum can. Which things will the magnet stick to? Make your predictions. Now, let's test. The paper clip? Click! It sticks. The paper cup? No. Magnets stick to iron, but not to paper. Say it with me. Magnets stick to iron, but not to paper. Wonderful! Ask a question. Does a magnet stick to a coin? No, it doesn't. Most coins don't have iron in them. Let's read Dr. Moss's magnet card. "Magnets stick to iron and steel. Steel has iron in it. Magnets don't stick to paper, wood, glass, plastic or aluminum. Every magnet has two ends, N and S. N and S pull together. N and N push away. Be careful! Keep magnets away from phones and computers." Isn't that interesting? Now, phonics. Magnetic. Magnetism. Experiment. Experimental. Listen. mag-NET-ic, MAG-ne-tism. Same family, different strong part. Let's do some magnetic experiments!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Welcome to the If-Then Science Quiz! Two teams. Red team and green team. I'm the quiz master. I will read the questions. Press the buzzer and answer with if. Here's an easy one. What happens if you drop a ball? If you drop a ball, it falls. Say it with me. If you drop a ball, it falls. Perfect! When your friend answers, you can say, That's right! Good guess! Let's read the quiz cards. "Question one: What happens if you heat ice? Question two: What happens if you mix blue and yellow? Question three: What happens if you put a magnet near a nail? Question four: What happens if you put an egg in very salty water? Question five: What happens if you put a full bottle of water in the freezer?" Do you know all the answers? I think you do! Answer in a full sentence. If you heat ice, it melts. Now, phonics review. Photography. Scientific. Electricity. Magnetic. Say the strong part loudly. Ready? Buzzers up. Let's start the quiz!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we are in the lab's storeroom. It's full of materials. Materials are the things we use to make other things. Wood. Glass. Metal. Plastic. Paper. Dr. Moss's chair is very old. What is it made of? This chair is made of wood. Say it with me. This chair is made of wood. Great! Made of tells us the material. You can still see the material. The window is made of glass. Ask a question. Is this spoon made of metal? Yes, it is. Here is the storeroom list. Let's read it. "Shelf A: Wooden blocks and wooden spoons. Shelf B: Glass jars and glass tubes. Be careful. Glass can break. Shelf C: Metal tools. Some of them are a little rusty. Shelf D: Plastic cups and sticky tape. Shelf E: Bumpy rocks from the mountain. Please clean the dusty shelves every Friday." It sounds like a busy storeroom! Now, phonics. Sticky. Bumpy. Rusty. Dusty. Stick plus y. Bump plus y. Add y, not e y. Let's find out what things are made of!

phonics.tipJa: shine → shiny（ぴかぴかの）、ice → icy（こおりの）、noise → noisy（うるさい）、juice → juicy（みずみずしい）。e で おわる ことばは e を とってから y を つける。shiney・icey は まちがい！

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Look at this piece of paper. Is it made of wood? Well, it doesn't look like wood. But paper is made from trees. Say it with me. Paper is made from trees. Excellent! Here's the difference. Made of: you can still see the material. This chair is made of wood. Made from: the material changed, and you can't see it anymore. Glass is made from sand. Dr. Moss has a model of a paper factory. Let's read the signs on the model. "Step one: Trees are cut into small chips. Step two: The chips are mixed with water. It's very noisy here! Step three: The wet mix is pressed flat. Step four: The paper is dried with hot rollers. Shiny paper and soft paper are made here. Step five: Old paper comes back. We can recycle old paper again and again." So, our notebooks, our books and even our boxes come from trees. Let's use paper carefully. Now, phonics. Shiny. Icy. Noisy. Juicy. Shine, take away the e, add y. Let's learn where things come from!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Behind the Green Laboratory, there's a small rice field. Dr. Moss grows rice here every year. Rice is grown in many parts of Japan. Say it with me. Rice is grown in many parts of Japan. Wonderful! Is grown means people grow it there. We can also say, Rice grows in wet fields. Apples are grown in Aomori. Let's read the sign next to the rice field. "Rice is grown in many parts of Asia. In Japan, people plant young rice plants in spring. The fields are full of water and mud. In summer, the plants grow tall and green in the sunny weather. In the fall, the rice turns gold, and people cut it. Niigata is famous for its rice." Let's think. What food is grown near your home? Maybe strawberries, or tea, or cabbages. Now, phonics. Sunny. Muddy. Spotty. Starry. Sun has a short u and one n. So, double the n and add y. Let's get muddy and plant some rice!

phonics.tipJa: -y の まとめ: cloud → cloudy（そのまま y）・salt → salty（そのまま y）・shine → shiny（e を とる）・sun → sunny（しいんを かさねる）。3つの きまりを くらべよう。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will be detectives. We will find out where things are made. Let's start with something everyone loves. Chocolate! Where is chocolate made? Say it with me. Where is chocolate made? Good! Chocolate is made in many countries. Japan makes chocolate, too. But the beans come from far away. Cacao beans are grown in hot countries, like Ghana. Let's read Dr. Moss's fact card. "Chocolate is made from cacao beans. Cacao trees like hot, sunny and rainy places near the equator. Many cacao beans are grown in Ghana and the Ivory Coast in West Africa. The beans are dried in the sun and sent to chocolate factories around the world. In the factories, the beans are roasted and mixed with sugar and milk." Wow. A chocolate bar travels a long way! Look at the label on a food package. You can often find the country. Now, phonics. Cloudy. Salty. Shiny. Sunny. Cloud plus y. Shine, drop the e, plus y. Sun, double the n, plus y. Let's be food detectives!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Welcome to the Mystery Box Quiz! Dr. Moss puts something in a box. You can ask questions, and Dr. Moss gives hints. Then you guess the material. First, ask, What is it made of? Then, guess. It's made of glass and metal. Say it with me. It's made of glass and metal. Super! You can ask yes or no questions, too. Is it made of plastic? No, it isn't. Let's read the hint cards for the first box. "Hint one: It's hard and shiny. Hint two: It's made of glass and metal. Hint three: You can see through the glass part. Hint four: Scientists use it every day to look at tiny things. Hint five: Its name starts with micro." Do you know the answer? Yes! It's a microscope! You can also use your own hints. It's soft. It's sticky. It's made of cotton. Now, phonics review. Sticky. Shiny. Muddy. Cloudy. Use these words as hints in our quiz. Let's open the mystery boxes!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will start a seed experiment. What do seeds need to start growing? Dr. Moss gives us three cups. Each cup has cotton and five bean seeds. Cup A: wet cotton, in a warm room. Cup B: dry cotton, in a warm room. Cup C: wet cotton, in the fridge. Make your prediction. Three days later, here are the results. Only the seeds in cup A started to grow. Seeds need water and warm air. Say it with me. Seeds need water and warm air. Great! The seeds in the dry cup didn't change. We need to keep the cotton wet. Let's read Dr. Moss's observation card. "Most seeds don't need light to start. They need water, air and the right temperature. When a seed drinks water, it gets bigger and softer. Then a tiny root pushes out." Hmm. The Sleeping Seed has water and warm air, but it's still sleeping. Maybe it needs something else. Now, phonics. Prediction. Reaction. Collection. Observation. Predict plus ion. Observe, drop the e, plus ation. Let's take care of our seeds!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Our bean seeds are growing! Today, we will move them into pots with soil and observe them every day. Plants grow in order. Let's learn the order. First, a root grows. Then, a stem grows. Say it with me. First, a root grows. Then, a stem grows. Wonderful! Next, two small leaves open. Isn't it interesting? The root grows down, and the stem grows up. Even if you turn the seed upside down, the root still grows down! Let's read a page from Dr. Moss's plant book. "How a bean plant grows. First, the seed drinks water and gets bigger. Then, the seed coat cracks, and a root grows down into the soil. Next, a stem grows up toward the light. After that, two small leaves open. Finally, more leaves grow, and the plant gets taller and taller." Use First, Then, Next, After that and Finally. They help us explain the order clearly. Now, phonics. Observation. Preparation. Collection. Prediction. Observe and prepare drop the e. Let's watch our plants grow!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Look at the lemon tree in the greenhouse. There's a little green caterpillar (いもむし) on a leaf. Dr. Moss says it will change a lot. A caterpillar becomes a butterfly. Say it with me. A caterpillar becomes a butterfly. Excellent! Becomes means changes into. Let's learn the steps. First, a butterfly lays an egg on a leaf. Then, a tiny caterpillar comes out and eats and eats. Next, the caterpillar makes a chrysalis. Let's read the life cycle poster. "The life of a swallowtail butterfly. Day 1: A butterfly lays a small yellow egg on a lemon leaf. Day 5: A tiny caterpillar comes out of the egg. It eats the leaves and grows bigger. Day 25: The caterpillar makes a chrysalis and stays very still. Day 35: A beautiful butterfly comes out. It dries its wings and flies away." Some butterflies even fly to warm places in the fall. That's called migration. Now, phonics. Migration. Rotation. Evaporation. Celebration. Migrate, take away t e, add tion. Let's watch our caterpillar change!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Two weeks ago, we put two bean plants in two places. One plant was by the sunny window. One plant was in a dark corner, in the shade. We gave both plants the same water. That's important. In a fair test, we change only one thing. Here are the results. The plant by the window was green and strong. The plant in the shade was pale and thin. Plants need sunlight to grow. Say it with me. Plants need sunlight to grow. Wonderful! Plants use sunlight to make their own food in their leaves. Let's read Riko's observation notes. "Window plant: The stem was 18 centimeters tall. It had six green leaves. It looked strong and healthy. Shade plant: The stem was very long and thin, but it was weak. The leaves were small and yellow. It leaned toward the window, because a little light came from there." So the dark plant was looking for light! Now, phonics. Evaporation. Observation. Prediction. Rotation. Listen. The strong part comes just before tion. Let's give our plants some sunlight!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! For two weeks, we watched our bean plants and wrote a growth diary every day. Today, you will share your diary. Use numbers to show the changes. On day five, the stem was three centimeters tall. Say it with me. On day five, the stem was three centimeters tall. Excellent! You can talk about leaves, too. On day ten, it had four leaves. And you can talk about how fast it grew. It grew two centimeters in three days. Let's read Kiko's diary. "Day 1: I planted my bean seed. Day 3: A small root came out. Day 5: The stem was three centimeters tall. Day 7: Two small leaves opened. Day 10: It had four leaves. The stem was eight centimeters tall. Day 14: The stem was twelve centimeters tall. It grew four centimeters in four days! My bean is growing fast." Great diary, Kiko! Remember to use the past tense. It was. It had. It grew. Now, phonics review. Prediction. Observation. Migration. Celebration. Let's present our growth diaries!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Big news! The Green Laboratory will have a science fair at the end of this world. Every team will do an experiment and present it. First, we need a good question. A good question is something you can test. Haru and Riko have an idea. Our question is, Do plants like music? Say it with me. Our question is, Do plants like music? Great! Next, think about what you will need. We will need two plants, a speaker and a ruler. And here's the most important question for a fair test. What will you change, and what will you keep the same? Let's read the team's plan. "Our question: Do plants like music? What we will change: One plant will hear music every day. The other plant will not. What we will keep the same: The same kind of plant, the same pot, the same water and the same sunlight. What we will measure: The height of the plants every morning." That's a very scientific plan. Now, phonics review. Microscope. Experiment. Scientist. Prediction. Let's plan our science fair projects!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Haru and Riko's experiment is going well. For two weeks, they played music for one plant. The other plant stayed in a quiet room. Now, let's tell people what we did. Use the past tense. We played music for one plant every day. Say it with me. We played music for one plant every day. Wonderful! Then explain the fair test. We gave both plants the same water and sunlight. And we measured the plants every morning. Let's read their measurement table. "Music plant: Day 1, five centimeters. Day 7, nine centimeters. Day 14, fourteen centimeters. Quiet plant: Day 1, five centimeters. Day 7, nine centimeters. Day 14, thirteen centimeters. Notes: Every morning, we checked both rooms with a thermometer. The temperature was the same for both plants. We played gentle piano music for one hour each day." Hmm. The music plant is one centimeter taller. Is that a big difference? Let's think about it next time. Now, phonics review. Thermometer. Measurement. Energy. Sunny. Let's do our experiments carefully!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today, we will write a lab report. A lab report has four parts. Purpose. Prediction. Result. Conclusion. Our report has four parts: purpose, prediction, result and conclusion. Say it with me. Our report has four parts: purpose, prediction, result and conclusion. Great! The purpose is why we did the experiment. The conclusion (けつろん) is what we learned. Let's read Riko's lab report. "Purpose: The purpose of our experiment was to find out about plants and music. Prediction: We predicted the music plant would grow taller. Result: After two weeks, the music plant was 14 centimeters tall. The quiet plant was 13 centimeters tall. Conclusion: The music plant grew a little more. But one centimeter is a very small difference. We only used two plants. We can't be sure yet. We need to try again with more plants." What an honest report! Good scientists don't jump to conclusions. They say, We can't be sure yet. Now, phonics review. Telescope. Equipment. Photography. Shiny. Observation. Let's write our lab reports!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Today is our goodbye tour of the Green Laboratory. Let's remember everything. In the safety room, we learned the rules. Wear your goggles. In the water room, we said, I predict the apple will float. And the egg floated in salt water! If you heat ice, it melts. In the storeroom, we said, It's made of wood. Paper is made from trees. And in the greenhouse, we said, Plants need sunlight to grow. We learned a lot in the Green Laboratory. Say it with me. We learned a lot in the Green Laboratory. Beautiful! Oh, wait! Kiko found a very old notebook in the storeroom. It belonged to Dr. Moss's grandfather. Let's read the last page. "I found the Sleeping Seed on a snowy mountain. Seeds from cold places are clever. They wait for winter. If the seed feels a long, cold winter, it knows that spring is coming. Then it can wake up." A cold winter! Seeds from cold places need cold first. Dr. Moss puts the seed in the fridge for a pretend winter. Now, phonics review. Thermostat. Environment. Magnetic. Muddy. Migration. Let's finish our goodbye tour!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Welcome to the World 23 Grand Review! Today is the Green Laboratory Science Fair. Every team will share their experiment. At the end of your talk, tell us the most exciting part. We found out something amazing! Say it with me. We found out something amazing! Fantastic! In this world, you learned so much. Wear your goggles. I can see tiny circles. The water is 20 degrees. I predict the apple will float. The result was surprising. If you heat ice, it melts. Magnets stick to iron. This chair is made of wood. Rice is grown in Japan. Seeds need water and warm air. Plants need sunlight to grow. Here is the science fair program. Let's read it. "Green Laboratory Science Fair. Part one: Float or Sink. Part two: Do Plants Like Music? Part three: The Dancing Raisins. Part four: Kiko and Birimo, The Sleeping Seed. Special guest: Dr. Moss." Now, phonics review. Microwave. Pedometer. Development. Scientific. Cloudy. Celebration. You are wonderful scientists. Let the science fair begin!
